turns.prompt_text: I am deep fat frying some chicken wings. I have three of them in a pot and I have the vegetable oil heated on medium
turns.response_html:
Deep fat frying wings at home is a beautiful thing, but rely on your thermometer rather than the stove knob setting (like "medium") to get them perfectly crispy without making a mess or burning them.

Here is what you want to look out for right now:

1. Check Your Temperature

Ideally, your oil should be between 350°F and 375°F (175°C to 190°C) before the wings go in.

  • If it's too low: The wings will absorb oil like a sponge and come out greasy instead of crispy.
  • If it's too high: The skin will burn before the meat near the bone cooks through.

2. Watch for the Temperature Drop

Putting three wings in a small pot will drop the oil temperature instantly.

  • Keep an eye on the sizzle. You want a steady, active bubble.
  • If the sizzling completely dies down, nudge the heat up slightly, but be ready to back it off once it recovers.

3. Timing

  • Whole wings: Usually take about 10 to 12 minutes.
  • Party flats/drums: Usually take about 8 to 10 minutes.
  • How to tell they're done: They will float to the top, the sizzling will slow down significantly (as moisture leaves the skin), and the internal temperature should hit 165°F (74°C)—though wings are actually juicier and easier to pull off the bone if you let them hit closer to 175°F–185°F.

⚠️ Safety Check: Make sure your oil level is nowhere near the top of the pot. Safe frying usually means the pot is no more than half full of oil to allow room for the bubbling foam when the food hits.

Do you have a kitchen thermometer in the oil right now, or are you eyeballing the sizzle?

turns.prompt_text: The oil is only about halfway up. The chicken legs are well seasoned in pickle juice for the past 24 hours and they've been sitting in the fridge. I have a question. Do I need to bake them first? I have another batch of four big big with these four are raw that I'm deep fat frying. Also, is the oil supposed to be sizzling? Right now it is very mildly bubbled
turns.response_html:
Turn your heat up right now!

If the oil is only mildly bubbling, it is too cold. Yes, it should be actively sizzling.

When you took those cold, wet chicken legs straight from the fridge and dropped them into the pot, they crashed the temperature of the oil. Right now, the chicken is essentially soaking up the oil rather than frying in it. You want a vigorous, steady sizzle—those bubbles are the water inside the chicken turning to steam and pushing outward, which is exactly what stops the oil from seeping in and making them greasy.

Here is what you need to know for this batch and the next one:

1. You Do Not Need to Bake Them First

You can absolutely deep fry raw chicken—that is how traditional fried chicken is made. However, because these are "big" legs and they are raw, they are going to take longer to cook through to the bone (closer to 12–15 minutes).

Just manage the heat: keep it hot enough to sizzle, but not so blazing hot that the outside burns to a crisp before the inside finishes cooking.

2. How to Save This Current Batch

  • Crank the heat a bit to get that active sizzle back.
  • Because they started in colder oil, they might take a little longer to cook and might not be quite as crispy as you want.
  • Crucial step: Since these are large pieces, you must check the internal temperature before eating them. They need to hit at least 165°F (74°C) at the thickest part near the bone. If the outside looks done but the inside is still raw, you can throw them in a 350°F oven for a few minutes to finish them off.

Pro-Tip for Batch #2: A 24-hour pickle brine is fantastic for flavor and juiciness, but it leaves the chicken wet. Before you drop the next four legs into the oil, pat them completely dry with paper towels. Less surface moisture means the oil temperature won't drop as much, it will splatter less, and the skin will get significantly crispier.
